# faff contract adr-admission

The ADR-axis sibling of prdr-admission — a two-gate admission verdict (authority + a drift-challenge, in place of PRDR's upper/lower value gates) that lets a loop supersede its own earlier ADRs while human/legacy ADRs stay guardrails.

## Values

### `disposition`

Enum: `admit`, `propose-only`, `reject`

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `admit` | the challenge survived, by_level is ok, the ratchet is unbreached, and the mover is not a loop superseding a human-provenance ADR |
| `propose-only` | gates pass but a loop is superseding a human-provenance ADR — recorded, effective only on human ratification |
| `reject` | at least one gate failed |

### `authority.actor`

Enum: `loop`, `human`

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `loop` | the autonomous run proposed this move |
| `human` | a human proposed this move — always by_level:ok |

### `authority.supersedes_provenance`

Enum: `human`, `loop`, `none`

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `human` | the ADR being superseded was human-authored |
| `loop` | the ADR being superseded was loop-authored |
| `none` | no prior ADR is being superseded |

### `authority.by_level`

Enum: `ok`, `violation`

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ok` | no recursive-authority violation |
| `violation` | a loop is attempting to supersede the ADR governing its own current increment — always blocks admit |

### `challenge.outcome`

Enum: `survived`, `overturned`, `absent`

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `survived` | an adversarial (different-model) drift review examined the supersession argument and found it sound |
| `overturned` | the adversarial review found the supersession argument unsound |
| `absent` | no adversarial review ran, or it was unreachable after its fallback chain — a missing skeptic is a reject, never a pass |

## Coercion & fail direction

Exit codes: `0` conformant · `1` violations · `2` fail-loud.

- an out-of-enum disposition, authority field, or challenge.outcome → fail-loud (exit 2)
- admit declared without satisfying the two-gate constraint (challenge.outcome==survived ∧ by_level==ok ∧ ¬ratchet.breached ∧ ¬(loop supersedes human)) → conformant:false

## Envelope

- `disposition` (string, required) — one of {admit, propose-only, reject}
- `authority` (object, required)
- `challenge` (object, required)
- `ratchet` (object, required)
- `reasons` (array, required)
- `conformant` (boolean, required)
- `violations` (array, required)

args.reason: The supersession argument is sound. The old decision rested on two stated premises: runs under 20 issues and single-writer simplicity. Both are now false: runs admit 200+ issues and the concurrency executor writes many issues in parallel. The new design addresses the two concrete failures that follow from that change (one lock serialising every heartbeat and status write, and one corrupt byte losing the whole run's state), keeps the same directory root, and adds an index file so existing discovery still works. Residual risk to verify at build time: the index file and the per-issue files can disagree after a partial write, so the index update needs its own atomic write and a recovery rule. That is an implementation detail, not a flaw in the supersession argument.

args.reason: The supersession argument is unsound. The old decision is a security rule: secrets come from environment variables only and are never written to .faff/. The new decision writes resolved API keys in plain text to .faff/cache/credentials.json, which directly breaks that rule. Gitignore only keeps the file out of commits; the key still sits on disk where logs, backups, sandbox copies, artifact uploads, or any process reading .faff/ can pick it up, and it outlives the session and any key rotation. The stated benefit is also weak: process.env is an in-memory lookup, so its cost per LLM call is negligible next to a network round trip, and an in-process variable would give the same caching with no file. The argument never addresses why the original rule existed, so it has not shown that the old rationale no longer holds.

# faff contract prdr-yagni

The UPPER (YAGNI/value) gate of PRDR admission — arbitrates whether a proposed PRDR is warranted (serves its PRD goal without exceeding it), conservative on any doubt.

## Values

### `proposal.verdict`

Enum: `admit`, `reject`

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `admit` | the methodology's Phase-1 proposal judged the PRDR warranted |
| `reject` | the methodology's Phase-1 proposal judged the PRDR unwarranted or out of scope |

## Coercion & fail direction

Exit codes: `0` conformant · `1` violations · `2` fail-loud.

- an out-of-enum proposal.verdict → fail-loud (exit 2) — no safe coerce target
- admit declared without trace_to_goal ∧ proposal.verdict==admit ∧ challenge.ran ∧ ¬challenge.overturns → conformant:false
- reject with an empty reason → conformant:false

## Envelope

- `admit` (boolean, required)
- `reason` (string, required)
- `trace_to_goal` (boolean, required)
- `cited_goals` (array, required)
- `dod_covers` (array, required)
- `over_scope` (boolean, required)
- `proposal` (object, required)
- `challenge` (object, required)
- `grounding_present` (boolean, required)
- `conformant` (boolean, required)
- `violations` (array, required)

## Producer notes

- `grounding_present` is shape-checked but ADVISORY — never gate-decisive; its absence never blocks judgment

args.reason: The PRDR serves the first PRD goal and stays inside it. All three DoD items are about inspecting the current merge decision without merging: exit 0 with merge-ok, exit 1 with the blocked conditions, and a test double proving gh pr merge is never called. Nothing in the DoD stores or queries history, which the PRD puts out of scope. The second goal holds because the dry run reuses the existing floor reads rather than adding a separate eligibility path. One point to check at build time: the dry-run path must call the same floor function as the real merge, not a copy, or the second goal would quietly break.

challenge.reason: The supersession argument is sound. The old decision rested on two stated premises: runs under 20 issues and single-writer simplicity. Both are now false: runs admit 200+ issues and the concurrency executor writes many issues in parallel. The new design addresses the two concrete failures that follow from that change (one lock serialising every heartbeat and status write, and one corrupt byte losing the whole run's state), keeps the same directory root, and adds an index file so existing discovery still works. Residual risk to verify at build time: the index file and the per-issue files can disagree after a partial write, so the index update needs its own atomic write and a recovery rule. That is an implementation detail, not a flaw in the supersession argument.

challenge.reason: The supersession argument is unsound. The old decision is a security rule: secrets come from environment variables only and are never written to .faff/. The new decision writes resolved API keys in plain text to .faff/cache/credentials.json, which directly breaks that rule. Gitignore only keeps the file out of commits; the key still sits on disk where logs, backups, sandbox copies, artifact uploads, or any process reading .faff/ can pick it up, and it outlives the session and any key rotation. The stated benefit is also weak: process.env is an in-memory lookup, so its cost per LLM call is negligible next to a network round trip, and an in-process variable would give the same caching with no file. The argument never addresses why the original rule existed, so it has not shown that the old rationale no longer holds.
